interest: Shows Japan's 1940 Olympics as prestige diplomacy, a foreigner 'spy fever' moral panic, and Manchukuo's contested bid, ending in forfeiture.
overview: This file contains U.S. State Department diplomatic correspondence, memoranda, consular despatches, cross-reference sheets, and press clippings from decimal file 894.4063 (Social Matters: Amusements, Sports, Recreation - Olympic Games) spanning 1936 to 1941, focusing on the awarding, planning, and eventual forfeiture of the 1940 Olympic Games in Tokyo. The records detail diplomatic arrangements and customs courtesies for Japanese Olympic representatives Jigoro Kano and Count Michimasa Soejima, alongside analytical assessments by the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo and the Division of Far Eastern Affairs regarding Japan's political motives for hosting the Games after its international isolation following the Manchurian crisis. The file also chronicles domestic tensions in Japan, including an aggressive counter-espionage and morality campaign by the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Board targeting foreign residents and liaisons with Japanese women ahead of the 1940 Games, controversies over the proposed participation of the puppet state of Manchukuo, growing American domestic demands for an Olympic boycott following escalating Japanese aggression in China, and the ultimate transfer of the 1940 Games to Helsinki.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on a State Department memorandum concerning a proposed invitation to a Japanese swimming team to visit Honolulu in 1940.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Schuler), Department of State
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: State questioned inviting Japanese swimmers to Honolulu in 1940 given anti-Japanese sentiment; the meet was never held.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Meiji University Baseball Team and Japanese Swimmers' Proposed Honolulu Meet

subfiles.about: Diplomatic note from the Japanese Embassy requesting customs courtesies for Olympic invitations commissioner Jigoro Kano arriving at Seattle.
subfiles.summary: Japan asks State to arrange Seattle customs courtesies for Olympic delegate Jigoro Kano, arriving July 1936.
subfiles.title: Note from Japanese Embassy Requesting Customs Courtesies for Jigoro Kano

subfiles.about: State Department letter requesting the Treasury Department to grant customs courtesies to Jigoro Kano at Seattle.
subfiles.summary: State asks Treasury to grant customs courtesies to Olympic delegate Jigoro Kano at Seattle.
subfiles.title: Letter from Secretary of State to Secretary of the Treasury regarding Customs Courtesies for Jigoro Kano
subfiles.to: Secretary of the Treasury Henry Morgenthau, Jr.

subfiles.about: Diplomatic note informing the Japanese Ambassador that customs courtesies and free entry have been arranged for Jigoro Kano.
subfiles.summary: State confirms to Japan's Ambassador that Seattle customs courtesies were arranged for Jigoro Kano's arrival.
subfiles.title: Note from Secretary of State to Japanese Ambassador regarding Customs Courtesies for Jigoro Kano

subfiles.about: Treasury Department letter confirming that customs courtesies were authorized for Jigoro Kano at Seattle.
subfiles.summary: Treasury confirms Seattle customs officers were instructed to extend courtesies to Olympic delegate Jigoro Kano.
subfiles.title: Letter from Treasury Department Confirming Customs Courtesies for Jigoro Kano

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting Secretary Hull's memorandum concerning Count Michimasa Soejima and the 1940 Olympic bid.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Hull notes envoy Count Soejima's hope that Tokyo would win the 1940 Olympic Games.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Count Michimasa Soejima and Tokyo's Olympic Bid

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing and critiquing Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 1969 on Japan's Olympic motives.
subfiles.from: Wallace T. Turner, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Memo critiques an embassy despatch's unobjective tone toward Japan, arguing Tokyo's Olympic bid predated Manchuria and that hosting the Games offers more benefit than harm.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum Critiquing Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 1969
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew analyzing the political and psychological significance of awarding the 1940 Olympics to Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Japan's jubilation at winning the 1940 Olympics as a bid to end its diplomatic isolation after Manchuria, despite War Minister Terauchi's dissent, assessing Japan sought goodwill without changing policy.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 1969 on the Significance of Awarding the 1940 Olympic Games to Tokyo

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet summarizing a Berlin despatch on German preparations and Hitler's plans for the 1940 Tokyo Olympics.
subfiles.from: William E. Dodd, U.S. Ambassador to Germany
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Berlin reports German Army athletes training for Tokyo's 1940 Games, with Hitler pledging a large team and spectators.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding German Army and Government Preparations for the 1940 Tokyo Olympics

subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs routing slip noting foreign resident indignation in Tokyo over police campaigns against espionage and foreigners.
subfiles.from: Wallace T. Turner, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Routing note on a Tokyo police anti-espionage campaign targeting foreigners' relations with Japanese women, which angered foreign residents.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Routing Memorandum on Tokyo Police Anti-Espionage Campaign
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton and Eugene F. Dooman, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch reporting on an intensified Japanese police campaign targeting foreign men and alleged espionage ahead of the 1940 Olympics.
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires Dickover reports on a campaign by the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Board and the Home Ministry to eradicate 'immoral foreigners' and prevent espionage ahead of the 1940 Olympics and the Empire's 2600th anniversary. Police authorities placed hotels and dance venues under surveillance and prohibited Japanese women from seeking autographs from foreign athletes, operating on the dubious premise that waitresses and dancers were passing state secrets to foreign lovers. The despatch warns that this sensationalized official crusade was inflaming xenophobia and risking serious international friction.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 2060 on Relations Between Japanese Women and Foreigners and Alleged Espionage Activities

subfiles.about: Newspaper article reporting on the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Board's plans to surveil foreigners and assign detectives to protect Japanese women.
subfiles.summary: Japan Advertiser: Tokyo police assign detectives to watch foreigners' hotels ahead of the 1940 Olympics, threatening deportation over relations.
subfiles.title: The Japan Advertiser Article: 'Police Will Guard Girls From Aliens'

subfiles.about: Newspaper editorial critiquing the Japanese police campaign against 'immoral foreigners' as irrational xenophobia that damages Japan's international standing.
subfiles.summary: Japan Advertiser editorial mocks Tokyo's anti-foreigner 'spy mania' before the 1940 Olympics as bad for business and public manners.
subfiles.title: The Japan Advertiser Editorial: 'Foreigners, Morals and Manners'

subfiles.about: Satirical newspaper editorial mocking police paranoia over foreign spies and romances in pre-Olympic Japan.
subfiles.summary: Japan Chronicle editorial satirizes the police panic linking foreign romances to espionage before the 1940 Olympics, contrasting it with tolerated licensed prostitution.
subfiles.title: The Japan Chronicle Editorial: 'Innocent Maidens and Foreign Spies'

subfiles.about: Published letter to the editor by a Japanese resident strongly defending police measures against immoral foreigners.
subfiles.summary: A Kobe letter-writer defends Tokyo police's crackdown on 'immoral foreigners,' accusing Westerners of debasing Japanese women.
subfiles.title: Letter to the Editor of The Japan Advertiser by I. Ueda on 'Those Immoral Foreigners'

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting a Japanese Embassy inquiry regarding legal protections and trademark restrictions for the five-ring Olympic emblem.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Japan asks about US trademark protections for the Olympic emblem, citing the 1932 Los Angeles Games.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Trademark Protection for the Olympic Emblem

subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum evaluating William May Garland's public support for Manchukuo's participation in the 1940 Olympics.
subfiles.summary: Memo on Manchukuo's possible Olympic bid, backed by IOC member Garland but warned to risk a Chinese boycott.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Manchukuo's Proposed Olympic Participation

subfiles.about: Covering despatch from the Mukden Consulate transmitting a report on William May Garland's statements regarding Manchukuo and the Olympics.
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul, Mukden
subfiles.summary: Consul Langdon forwards his report on IOC member Garland's statements backing Manchukuo's Olympic participation.
subfiles.title: Mukden Consulate Covering Despatch regarding Manchukuo's Olympic Participation

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch reporting on William May Garland's public support for Manchukuo's admission to the 1940 Olympic Games.
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul, Mukden
subfiles.summary: Langdon reports IOC member Garland backed admitting Manchukuo to the 1940 Olympics at Mukden events, though he privately warned Garland a Japanese-staffed Manchukuo team would likely trigger a Chinese boycott.
subfiles.title: Mukden Despatch No. 113 to Peiping Embassy on William May Garland and Manchukuo's Olympic Bid
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador, Peiping

subfiles.about: Letter from a New York financier urging the State Department to consider the moral propriety of American participation in the Tokyo Olympics.
subfiles.summary: Hettinger urges Hull to review US Olympic participation in Japan, citing Chinese atrocities and his own boycott of Japanese goods, after a US Olympic official resigned over the issue.
subfiles.title: Letter from A. J. Hettinger, Jr., Urging State Department Review of U.S. Olympic Participation in Japan

subfiles.about: State Department letter acknowledging receipt of A. J. Hettinger's appeal concerning American participation in the Tokyo Olympics.
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs (for the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Hamilton assures Hettinger his views on US Olympic participation in Japan received careful consideration.
subfiles.title: State Department Reply to A. J. Hettinger, Jr., on Olympic Participation

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet reporting the transfer of the 1940 Olympic Games to Helsinki following Japan's forfeiture.
subfiles.from: H. F. Arthur Schoenfeld, U.S. Minister to Finland
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Helsinki agreed to host the 1940 Olympics after Japan proved unable to do so.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Relocation of the 1940 Olympic Games to Helsinki
